problem: Classical mobile-robot navigation treats traversability as a geometry problem (map, then plan collision-free paths). It therefore misjudges non-geometric affordances: tall grass looks like an obstacle, and concrete versus grass is not separable by geometry. Semantic or traversability learning methods instead rely on human labels or SLAM-derived labels, and end-to-end RL navigation typically needs on-policy data or simulation, or only learns collision avoidance (GCG). CAPs also needed human supervision for non-collision objectives.
motivation: Physical attributes such as traversability, bumpiness and collision can be measured by the robot's own onboard sensors (IMU, LIDAR, odometry) after the fact. Past experience can therefore retrospectively self-label data, with no humans or simulation involved. Since real-world data is expensive, an off-policy learner that can reuse all data from any collection policy lets the robot keep improving from autonomously gathered experience.
key_idea: Autonomously collect off-policy real-world driving data with a time-correlated random policy, then self-label future events (collision, bumpiness, position) from onboard sensors. From this, train an image-plus-action-sequence-conditioned predictive model and plan through it with MPC under a user-specified reward.
insight: Letting the robot learn event predictors from proprioceptive and sensor outcomes, rather than from geometry, captures affordances that geometry gets wrong. BADGR learns that tall grass is traversable where the 2D-LIDAR policy gets trapped or detours (BADGR reached the goal 1.2× faster on average off-road). It also learns from camera images alone that concrete paths are smoother than grass. The bumpiness term matters: in the urban task, removing the bumpy cost raises average bumpiness from 8.7±4.4 to 15.0±3.4, worse than LIDAR's 13.3. The self-improvement study (figure only) shows that three hours of target-domain data plus the original data beats both the zero-shot model and a target-domain-only model, so prior off-policy data accelerates adaptation. The authors also report that a warm-started, reward-weighted, time-correlated zeroth-order optimizer (from Nagabandi et al.) was needed for good planning; random shooting or CEM was insufficient.
method: Robot platform: Clearpath Jackal with two forward 170° FOV 640×480 cameras, 2D LIDAR, IMU, GPS, compass and wheel encoders, plus an onboard Jetson TX2. It is commanded by linear and angular velocity setpoints.

Autonomous off-policy data collection: a time-correlated random-walk velocity policy explores. LIDAR (urban) or IMU (off-road) collision/stuck detection triggers an automatic back-up-and-rotate reset; humans intervene only for catastrophes such as flips. Data is subsampled to 4 Hz.

Self-supervised event labelling: collision comes from LIDAR proximity (urban) or a sudden IMU acceleration/angular-velocity drop (off-road). Bumpiness is IMU angular-velocity magnitude above a threshold. Position comes from a wheel-odometry + IMU state estimator.

Action-conditioned predictive model f_θ(o_t, a_{t:t+H}): a CNN + FC encoder on the current RGB image initializes an LSTM that consumes H future actions. FC heads predict all K events at each of the H steps, trained with cross-entropy (discrete) or MSE (continuous) losses.

Reward design: R = −Σ [R_COLL + α_POS·R_POS + α_BUM·R_BUM]. Every term lies in [0,1], and collision dominates: if a collision is predicted, all terms are set to 1. R_POS is the normalized angle between predicted position and the GPS goal.

MPC planning: a zeroth-order stochastic optimizer (Nagabandi et al.) samples N time-correlated action sequences around a warm-started running estimate (noise σ, correlation β). It updates the estimate by an exp(γ·R) reward-weighted average and executes the first action.

setting.backbone: CNN + FC image encoder feeding an action-conditioned LSTM event predictor (trained from scratch) + sampling-based MPC planner
setting.training_data: 42 hours of autonomously collected real-world off-policy data (34 h urban, 8 h off-road), ~720,000 datapoints at 4 Hz. Collected with a time-correlated random policy and self-labelled from onboard sensors; no human labels or simulation. The self-improvement study adds 3 h of target-area data.
setting.observation: monocular forward RGB camera image (170° FOV) + goal GPS coordinate; the onboard wheel-odometry/IMU state estimator supplies position for the goal-heading reward
setting.action_space: continuous linear and angular velocity commands (H-step action sequences planned with MPC)
setting.privileged: none (only a single goal GPS coordinate is given; LIDAR/IMU are used for training labels, not as policy input)

numbers.extra: 5 start locations × 5 runs each = 25 runs; real robot; uses camera images only (baseline LIDAR policy uses 2D LIDAR)
ablation: reward without bumpiness term; 25 runs

numbers_note: Only the urban experiment has a numeric table (Fig. 6). The off-road experiment (Fig. 8, 5 starts × 5 runs), the self-improvement study (Fig. 11: zero-shot / finetuned / target-domain-only) and the novel-environment generalization (Fig. 12) are reported only as trajectory plots and qualitative text. The only other number is 'BADGR reached the goal 1.2× faster on average compared to the LIDAR policy' off-road; the Fig. 10 caption cites 1.5× faster for one example. The Fig. 11 caption appears to swap the 'finetuned' and 'target domain only' labels relative to the main text. Evaluation is not a standard embodied-navigation benchmark.
results: In the urban goal-reaching task, BADGR reached the goal in 25/25 runs (100%) with average bumpiness 8.7±4.4. The 2D-LIDAR geometric policy also reached the goal in 25/25 runs but had bumpiness 13.3±2.9. The naive straight-to-goal policy succeeded in only 5/25 runs (20%). Off-road, BADGR almost always reached the goal, while LIDAR got trapped by tall grass it labelled untraversable. BADGR was 1.2× faster than LIDAR on average. BADGR also generalized to three novel environments and improved after 3 h of autonomously gathered target-area data.
limitations: Data collection still needs periodic human resets (e.g., when the robot flips), and the method assumes experiencing collisions is acceptable.
Improvement requires gathering a non-negligible amount of new data and retraining from scratch rather than adapting online.

Evaluated only in static environments with small real-world trial counts; off-road, self-improvement and generalization results are qualitative or figure-only, with no dynamic agents (pedestrians/cars).

CAPs (Composable Action-Conditioned Predictors, Kahn et al. 2018)
PDDM zeroth-order MPC optimizer (Nagabandi et al. 2019)
compares_to: LIDAR policy (2D-LIDAR geometric goal-reaching with collision avoidance)
